items.title: Level 1: Interview words you will meet
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Before you read about interviews, it helps to know the words that are used. A candidate is the person applying for the job. That is you. An interviewer is a person who asks the questions. In the Civil Service you will usually be seen by a panel, which is a small group of interviewers, often two or three people. One person usually leads and the others take notes. The advert lists the behaviours, which are the things the Civil Service wants to see you do at work, such as working well with other people. Some adverts also list strengths, which are the things you do well and enjoy doing. The example you give in an answer is a real thing that happened to you. A popular way to tell an example is the STAR method, which stands for Situation, Task, Action and Result. After the interview the panel gives each candidate a score. If you are unsuccessful you can ask for feedback, which is comments on how you did. If you pass but there is no vacancy yet, you may be put on a reserve list. If you are successful you get a conditional offer, which means the job is yours as long as the pre-employment checks go well. These checks include things like proof of who you are and your right to work in the UK. The words are simple, and once you know them the guidance becomes much easier to follow.

items.title: Level 1: The interview invitation
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: When the Civil Service wants to interview you, they send an invitation. You will often get this by email, and you may also see a message in your Civil Service Jobs account. Read it as soon as you can. The invitation usually tells you the date and time of your interview, how it will be held, and who to contact if you have a problem. Many Civil Service interviews are now held by video call, but some are held in a building, which is often called an office or an assessment centre. The invitation may name the video tool, such as Microsoft Teams, or give you a web link to click. It will say how long the interview is likely to last. Many interviews last somewhere between 30 minutes and an hour, though the exact length depends on the job. The invitation also explains how to ask for adjustments. An adjustment is a change that makes the interview fairer for you, for example extra time because of a health condition. You should always reply to confirm that you can attend. If you cannot make the date, contact the recruitment team straight away and explain. Do not simply ignore the message. Keep the invitation safe, because it holds details you may need on the day, such as a phone number to call if your link does not work. If you are asked to bring identity documents, check which ones are needed and find them early.

items.title: Level 1: Who is on the panel
items.body: A Civil Service interview is usually carried out by a panel. The panel is a small group, often two or three people, though the number can vary from department to department. They are normally people who work in the area you want to join, or who understand the job well. One member of the panel often leads the interview and asks most of the questions. The other members listen, ask follow-up questions and write notes. The note-taking is not rude. It is how they remember what you said so they can score you fairly. The panel asks the same set of questions of every candidate for the same job. This is done on purpose, so that the process is fair and everyone has the same chance. The panel scores each candidate against the criteria in the advert. They are not trying to catch you out. They want to find the best people, and many panel members hope that you will do well. A panel member may smile, nod or look down at their notes while you talk. Do not worry if their face does not show what they are thinking, because they are trained to stay neutral and to avoid giving hints. When you are introduced, say hello to everyone, speak clearly, and look at the person who asked the question as you begin your answer. You may also look at the others now and then.

items.title: Level 1: Behaviours and Success Profiles
items.body: The Civil Service uses a framework called Success Profiles to decide what each job needs. It describes five things that can be looked at when hiring: behaviours, strengths, ability, technical skills and experience. A job advert will say which of these will be assessed. At entry level the interview is often built around behaviours and sometimes strengths. Behaviours are the actions and skills that lead to doing a job well. There are nine Civil Service behaviours: Seeing the Big Picture, Changing and Improving, Making Effective Decisions, Leadership, Communicating and Influencing, Working Together, Developing Self and Others, Managing a Quality Service, and Delivering at Pace. Not every job tests all nine. A job advert usually lists only the ones that matter most, and for an Administrative Officer role these are often Working Together, Communicating and Influencing, Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace, but check each advert. Working Together means building good relationships and helping colleagues. Communicating and Influencing means explaining things clearly and listening. Managing a Quality Service means paying attention to detail and making sure people get a good result. Delivering at Pace means getting work done on time and keeping going when things get hard. The advert tells you what to prepare, so read it carefully and list the behaviours before you plan your examples.

items.title: Level 1: The STAR method
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: STAR is a simple way to tell an example so that the panel can follow it. It has four parts. The first part is Situation. Here you say where you were and what was going on, for example 'I was working on the front desk at a busy dental surgery.' Keep this short. The second part is Task. This is your job or goal in that situation, for example 'I had to make sure every patient was booked in on time.' The third part is Action. This is what you did, step by step, and it is the longest and most important part. Use the word 'I', not 'we', because the panel is scoring you and not your team. The fourth part is Result. This is what happened because of what you did, for example 'All patients were seen on time and the manager thanked me.' If you can, add a number or a clear outcome, and say what you learned. Some people add a second R for Reflection, which is what you would do differently next time. A good example is a real one. It can come from work, college, volunteering, caring for family or any other part of life. Practise your examples out loud before the interview, using short notes rather than a script, so that your answer sounds natural.

items.title: Level 1: Strengths questions
items.body: Some Civil Service interviews include strengths-based questions. These are different from behaviour questions. Behaviour questions ask what you have done in the past. Strengths questions ask about what you enjoy and what you are naturally good at. Examples are 'What are you best at?', 'What do you do when you are under pressure?' and 'What gives you the most energy?' These questions are often asked quickly, one after another, and the panel expects short answers. There are no tricks and no single right answer. The panel watches for energy and honesty. If you light up when you talk about helping people, they will notice. If you try to give the answer you think they want, it can sound false. A strength is not just something you can do. It is something you enjoy doing and that gives you energy, so you do it well without effort. A weakness, on the other hand, may be something you can do but find tiring. Before the interview, think about what people thank you for, what you find easy, and what you lose track of time doing. Then match your strengths to the job. If the job is full of detailed paperwork, it helps to know whether you actually like that. Do not memorise lines for strengths questions, because over-rehearsed answers sound flat. Be yourself, speak naturally and keep your answers short.

items.title: Level 1: Video interviews
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Many Civil Service interviews are held by video call, so it is important to be ready. A few days before, check that your internet connection, camera, microphone and speakers all work. Many people do a test call with a friend. Choose a quiet room with a plain background, and sit at a table or desk rather than on a bed or sofa. Put your device on something steady so the picture does not wobble, and make sure the camera is at about eye level. Face a window or a lamp so that your face is lit; a bright window behind you will make you look dark. Close other programs on your computer and turn off notifications, so that nothing pops up or makes a noise. Put your phone on silent, and tell the people you live with that you must not be disturbed. If you have young children or pets, arrange cover in advance. Dress as you would for an interview in an office. On the day, join the call a few minutes early, and have the invitation, your identity documents, a glass of water and your short notes close by if notes are allowed. Look at the camera when you speak, not only at the screen, and speak a little more slowly than normal. If the connection fails, stay calm and use the phone number in the invitation to contact the recruitment team.

items.title: Level 1: Giving a good answer
items.body: A good interview answer is clear, honest and specific. Start by listening to the whole question. Do not rush in before the panel has finished speaking. It is fine to pause for a few seconds to think, and a calm pause shows confidence. If you did not hear or understand the question, ask politely for it to be repeated or explained. Then answer the question that was asked, not a different one you prepared. Use a real example, say 'I' when you describe what you did, and finish with the result. Most answers should last about two minutes. One sentence is too short and ten minutes is too long. Speak at a steady pace and in a clear voice. If you tend to speak very fast when nervous, slow down on purpose. Be honest about your experience. If you do not know something, say so rather than guessing, and say how you would find out. Avoid criticising a former employer or colleague, as this can look unprofessional. Panels like to hear about what you learned, even from things that did not go perfectly. At the end of an answer you can stop, or check with 'Does that answer your question?' if you are unsure. The panel may then ask a follow-up question, called a probe, to get more detail. A probe is a normal part of the interview and not a sign that you did badly.

items.title: Level 1: Feeling nervous
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Nearly everyone feels nervous before an interview, including people who do it often. A little nervousness is normal and can even help you to concentrate. The best way to feel calmer is to prepare. Know the date, time and format, and plan your journey or your video set-up well in advance. Read the advert and prepare a handful of real examples. On the day, get a good night's sleep, eat something and drink water. Arrive or log in early so you are not rushing. Before you go in, breathe slowly: in through the nose for four seconds, then out through the mouth for six. This helps to slow a racing heart. During the interview, it is fine to take a sip of water and pause. If your mind goes blank, do not panic. You can say 'Could I take a moment to think?' and look at your notes if they are allowed. You can also ask the panel to repeat the question, which buys you a few more seconds. If you realise your example does not fit, you can say so and move to a better one. The panel will not mark you down for being human. Remember that they want to meet the real you. Try to treat the interview as a conversation about your work and your skills, not a test of your worth. Afterwards, reward yourself and note what went well.

As a reason to ask for a later date

questions.hint: Nearly everyone is nervous, and a little can help.

options.text: Revise until late at night
Avoid thinking about it
Read the advert at the last minute
Prepare in advance

questions.hint: Preparation reduces anxiety.

options.text: Drinking strong coffee
Telling yourself repeatedly to calm down
Breathing in slowly and out for longer
Practising your answers faster

questions.hint: Slow breathing calms your body.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible habit the night before an interview?

options.text: Learn some new answers
Rest well and go to bed at a normal time
Revise until midnight
Cut down on food

questions.hint: Sleep helps you think clearly.

questions.prompt: What can you say if your mind goes blank?

options.text: I am sure I did this once
Can we move to a different question?
Could I take a moment to think?
Sorry, I have not got an answer

questions.hint: A polite request for time is accepted.

options.text: Ask for the question to be repeated
Answer a different question you know
Say the question quietly to yourself
Start with a long introduction

questions.hint: Asking to repeat the question gives you thinking time.

options.text: Take a sip of water and pause
Ask to go back to the first question
Ask the panel to move on without you
Switch off your camera for a minute

options.text: Say so and move to a better example
Stop the interview
Carry on with it anyway
Ask the panel to choose an example

questions.prompt: Why should you arrive or log in early?

options.text: So you can watch other candidates
So you can ask the panel for tips
So you are not rushing
So you can choose a better time slot

questions.hint: Being early keeps you calm.

items.title: Level 1: Questions at the end
items.body: At the end of most Civil Service interviews, the panel will ask whether you have any questions for them. This is a normal part of the interview, and it is a chance to show that you are interested in the job. It is a good idea to prepare one or two questions beforehand, because it is hard to think of good ones on the spot. Good questions are about the work, the team and what the first weeks will be like. For example: 'What does a typical day look like for someone in this team?' or 'What training do new starters get?' or 'What would you hope someone in this role achieves in their first six months?' If the panel has already answered your questions during the interview, you can say so politely and perhaps ask a different one. Avoid asking about things that are in the advert, such as the salary, working hours or holiday, at this point, because these details are normally given to you later or can be found out from the advert. It is also best not to ask 'Did I get the job?' as the panel cannot tell you on the spot. It can be useful to ask when you will hear back, if the invitation does not say. At the end, thank the panel for their time. Say 'Thank you very much, I enjoyed talking to you' in your own words. A warm, polite finish leaves a good last impression.

questions.prompt: What will the panel usually ask at the end of the interview?

options.text: Whether you want to change your answers
Whether you accept the job
Whether you have any questions for them
Whether you are happy with your score

questions.hint: Most panels invite your questions at the end.

questions.prompt: Why is it a good idea to prepare questions in advance?

options.text: It makes the interview longer
Panels require a written list
It is hard to think of good ones on the spot
You are scored on how many you ask

questions.hint: Preparing helps you ask something useful.

options.text: Who else did you interview?
What training do new starters get?
Can I leave early on Fridays?
What is everyone else's salary?

questions.hint: A question about training shows interest in the job.

questions.prompt: What topics are best for questions to the panel?

options.text: How soon you can take holiday
The work, the team and the first weeks
The panel's home life
Gossip about other candidates

questions.hint: Questions about the work show you care about the job.

options.text: Ask for a repeat of earlier answers
Ask about something already covered
Say you have none and end the call
Say so politely and perhaps ask another

questions.hint: It is fine to say they have been answered.

options.text: What would success look like in this role?
Did I get the job?
What does a typical day look like?
When will I hear the outcome?

questions.hint: The panel cannot normally tell you the result on the spot.

options.text: Whether the panel enjoyed the day

When you are likely to hear the outcome

options.text: End the call immediately
Ask for your score
Thank the panel for their time
Tell them how you think you did

questions.hint: A warm thank you leaves a good last impression.

options.text: The panel is not allowed to discuss the job

questions.hint: Pay and conditions are usually covered in the advert or offer.

items.title: Level 1: Adjustments and fairness
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: The Civil Service wants interviews to be fair for everyone. If you have a disability, a health condition, or a need such as dyslexia, you can ask for adjustments. These are changes that help you to show what you can do. Examples include extra time, a break during the interview, having the questions in writing, a quiet room, or having a support person with you. To ask, use the contact details in your invitation or in your Civil Service Jobs application. Ask as early as you can, because it can take time to arrange. You do not have to describe your condition in detail, but you should explain what would help. The Civil Service also uses the Disability Confident scheme. If you apply under it and meet the minimum criteria for the job, you are normally offered an interview. This is called the guaranteed interview scheme. It does not mean you are guaranteed the job. You still have to do well at the interview. Interviews are also run in a way that avoids unfair treatment. Panels are trained, they use the same questions for everyone, and they score against set criteria. The Civil Service also welcomes people from all backgrounds, and you do not need a degree for an Administrative Officer role. If you feel you have been treated unfairly, you can raise it with the recruitment team, and you can follow the complaints process.

questions.prompt: What is an 'adjustment' in recruitment?

options.text: A change that helps you show what you can do
A special advantage that guarantees the job
A change to the job's duties
A lower score threshold for some candidates

questions.hint: Adjustments help make the process fair for you.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of an adjustment?

options.text: Being told the answers in advance
Easier questions than other candidates
A higher score for each answer
Extra time in the interview

questions.hint: Extra time is a common example.

questions.prompt: How should you ask for an adjustment?

options.text: Use the contact details in the invitation
Wait and ask the panel on the day
Tell the panel only after the interview
Mention it only after you receive an offer

questions.hint: The invitation says who to contact.

questions.prompt: Why is it best to ask for an adjustment early?

options.text: It can take time to arrange
Panels give higher marks for early requests
It lets you choose your own interview date
Late requests are never accepted

questions.hint: Early requests give time to arrange them.

questions.prompt: What does the Disability Confident guaranteed interview scheme offer?

options.text: Skipping all the pre-employment checks
A higher pay band than other applicants
The job offered without any interview at all
An interview if you meet the minimum criteria

questions.hint: The scheme gives an interview if you meet the minimum criteria.

questions.prompt: After a guaranteed interview, what decides whether you get the job?

options.text: How well you do at the interview
The date on which you applied
The order in which people were interviewed
Whether you mentioned your condition

questions.hint: The scheme guarantees an interview, not an offer.

questions.prompt: What qualifications does an Administrative Officer role usually ask for?

options.text: At least two A levels or equivalent
A professional qualification in administration
Usually none, as it is an entry-level role
A degree in a relevant subject such as business

questions.hint: Administrative Officer roles are entry level.

questions.prompt: How do panels keep interviews fair?

options.text: Same questions, scored against set criteria
Letting the lead panel member choose a favourite
Different questions chosen for each person
Scoring based on first impressions

questions.hint: Fixed criteria and common questions make it fair.

questions.prompt: Who can you contact if you feel you were treated unfairly?

options.text: The company that makes the video software
A different department's HR team
The other candidates
The recruitment team

questions.hint: The recruitment team can look into your concern.

items.title: Level 1: After the interview
items.body: After the interview, the panel talks about each candidate and scores them against the criteria in the advert. The recruitment team then makes decisions and tells candidates the result. This can take from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how many people were interviewed. While you wait, try not to replay every answer in your head. If you are successful you will get a conditional offer. This means the job is yours as long as the pre-employment checks are completed satisfactorily. These checks often include proof of your identity, your right to work in the UK, references from past employers or teachers, and a check of your criminal record at the basic level. Some roles need extra security checks. Do not resign from your current job until you receive a formal offer that is no longer conditional. If you pass but there are more successful candidates than jobs, you may be put on a reserve list. This means you could be offered a similar job if one becomes free within a set time. If you are not successful, ask for feedback. Feedback tells you what went well and what to improve, and it is one of the most useful things you can receive. Being turned down is common. It does not mean you are not good enough. Each application gives you new examples and more practice, so use the feedback and apply again.

questions.prompt: What does the panel do after the interview?

options.text: Scores each candidate against the criteria
Sends all the notes to the candidates
Chooses the candidate who talked the most
Asks candidates to rate themselves

questions.hint: Scoring against criteria is how decisions are made.

questions.prompt: What is a conditional offer?

options.text: An offer that lasts only for the trial week
A job offer that depends on checks being completed
An offer that can be withdrawn at any time for no reason
An offer that is final and cannot change

questions.hint: Conditional means subject to pre-employment checks.

Proof of identity and right to work
A full medical examination of fitness
An exam on Civil Service history

Not until you have a firm, unconditional offer
Before you submit any application at all
Straight after the interview ends if it went well

questions.hint: Wait until the offer is no longer conditional.

options.text: You must wait for the whole process to restart
You are offered the job automatically later
You may be placed on a reserve list
You are asked to repeat the interview

questions.hint: Reserve lists hold passed candidates for future jobs.

questions.prompt: If you are unsuccessful, what can you ask for?

options.text: A re-mark by a different panel
Feedback
A second interview straight away
A guaranteed place on the reserve list

questions.hint: Feedback tells you how to improve.

questions.prompt: How should you see being turned down for a job?

options.text: As common, and a chance to learn and try again
As proof you are unsuited to the Civil Service
As a sign the panel was unfair
As a reason never to apply again

questions.hint: Many people succeed after more than one application.

questions.prompt: How long can it take to hear a result?

options.text: A few days to a few weeks
Always on the same day
Always within an hour
Always about a year

questions.hint: Timing depends on how many people were interviewed.

options.text: Phone the panel every day
Replay every answer repeatedly
Note what went well and carry on with normal life
Stop applying anywhere else

questions.hint: Reflecting calmly helps you improve.
